summary:
Gauteng's documented record of violence against transgender people rests on a single recent case. Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old transgender woman from Soshanguve who was living in Winterveld (both in Tshwane), was attacked at about 1:30 am on 26 December 2024 in a tavern in Tshwane. A man had been saying that gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live'; he smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette and told her 'I told you I'm gonna kill you'. The cuts to her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead were stitched after treatment at Kgabo Clinic. She opened an assault case at Dube Police Station, which had shown no progress when MambaOnline reported on 6 January 2025. The incident is the province's most recent documented trans-specific hate crime on record.

On 10 November 2025 the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, sitting as an Equality Court under the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act, delivered judgment in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075). The court found that the Department of Correctional Services had engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of a transgender woman inmate by refusing to allow her to express her gender identity and by denying her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy. It held that the right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense, and ordered the Department to implement the required accommodations and to enforce its own standard operating procedures for transgender inmates. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling on 14 November 2025. The orders are enforceable against the Department in the province, giving trans people in Gauteng an operational equality-court remedy for discrimination of this kind.

The same judgment records the only documented determination of how transgender prisoners are housed in Gauteng. Mokoena, a transgender woman serving a life sentence at Johannesburg Correctional Centre, was initially held in the Medium A section, where she could express her gender identity through long hair, makeup and women's clothing. She was later moved to the Medium C section, and at the time of judgment was held in C Single Section, a segregated unit used for solitary confinement, and was accommodated with cisgender male cellmates despite asking for a single cell; she was first housed with two cisgender gay men and then with one cisgender man, an arrangement the Department justified by overcrowding. The court found that its standard operating procedures prescribe accommodation appropriate to gender identity where that is feasible and safe, that no basis existed for refusing her single accommodation, and ordered that she be held in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity and that the procedures be enforced.

For a transgender visitor, the risk documented in Gauteng concentrates in unprovoked violence against visibly transgender people and in the police response to it, while the province's courts have ordered enforceable protections for a transgender person in custody.
tangentialFactors:
The province's own hate-crime evidence base is a research study rather than an enforcement record. 'Hate Crimes Against Gay and Lesbian People in Gauteng: Prevalence, Consequences and Contributing Factors' was conducted in 2003/04 by OUT LGBT Well-being with the University of South Africa Centre for Applied Psychology, under the Joint Working Group research initiative, with authors Wells and Polders; partner organisations included Behind the Mask, Triangle Project, GALA and the Durban Lesbian & Gay Community & Health Centre. It is described as the first representative quantitative provincial hate-crime study in South Africa.

A 2016 Love Not Hate campaign review, hosted by GALA and conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being, measures levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally and records that only three quantitative studies of hate crime against LGBT people have ever been carried out; the 2003/04 Gauteng study is one of them. The province's hate-crime baseline therefore rests on a study more than two decades old, drawn from gay and lesbian respondents rather than transgender people.
localsOnly:
For transgender people held in correctional facilities in Gauteng, the Mokoena judgment is the operative protection: it converts the Department of Correctional Services' own standard operating procedures for transgender inmates into enforceable orders at Johannesburg Correctional Centre, covering gender-affirming hormone therapy at state expense, clothing and cosmetics expressing gender identity, accommodation and single-cell placement.

Residents who report anti-trans violence to the police face an enforcement gap in the documented case. The assault case opened at Dube Police Station in Tshwane after the 26 December 2024 attack had shown no progress when it was reported on 6 January 2025.

The Gauteng Division of the High Court sits as an Equality Court, and it has granted relief in a case of discrimination against a transgender person, which is the mechanism available to residents of the province bringing discrimination or harassment complaints.
outOfScopeNotes:
No statute specific to Gauteng on gender recognition, identity documents or facility access appears in the source inventory; those matters are set at national level, and the province's record here is judicial and incident-based.

The date of delivery of the Mokoena judgment is not fully resolved: the Human Rights Commission's statement gives 10 November 2025 as the date of the ruling and 14 November 2025 as the date of the statement welcoming it.

The outcome of the assault case opened at Dube Police Station after the 26 December 2024 attack, including whether any arrest resulted in prosecution, is not recorded in the inventory.

No provincial rate or count of violence against transgender people is available in the sources, so no comparison with Gauteng's general homicide rate can be made.
